claim: When a long passage (a derivation, a program, a news story or a poem) is written into a language model's weights by splitting it into segments and editing them in sequence with a locate-and-edit method, placing segment boundaries at the tokens the unedited model finds most surprising, rather than every fixed number of tokens, makes the edited model reproduce the new passage more faithfully. Supported only if, using the same underlying editor, it gives higher average BLEU and higher average BERTScore than fixed-window segmentation on a seven-domain long-form editing benchmark for each of three different LLMs, and higher scores on two further editing benchmarks (unstructured question answering and counterfactual facts); and if on a set of long chain-of-thought math answers, longer than anything in that benchmark, it scores higher in every bin of answer length and of reasoning-word density.

experiments: Fix the editing pipeline both segmentation schemes share. Setup: autoregressive long-form editing on top of MEMIT: split the target answer into segments; for each segment, take the hidden state at the token just before it at the edited MLP layers as the key and optimise a perturbation to that layer's output (Adam, learning rate 0.5, up to 20 steps, norm constraint) that maximises the segment's likelihood given the question and the earlier segments; then apply one batched least-squares weight update using key covariance from 100,000 Wikipedia samples. The only change under test is where boundaries go: every fixed number of tokens, or at the k highest peaks of per-token surprisal (-log2 p of each answer token under the unedited model given its prefix), with k = ceil(length / 40) and a rule forcing one boundary in the first three tokens. Score the edited model's answer against the target with BLEU and BERTScore (all-MiniLM-L6-v2).

Compare on a multi-domain long-form editing benchmark. Setup: EditEverything (math, code, physics, chemistry, biology, news, poetry) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-2-7B and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, against triple editors MEMIT and AlphaEdit and fixed-window AnyEdit, both long-form methods on the MEMIT base. Result: surprisal boundaries give the best total BLEU / BERTScore on every model: 75.00 / 94.50 vs AnyEdit 72.64 / 94.23 (Llama-3.1), 50.13 / 87.66 vs 42.30 / 86.33 (Llama-2), 85.33 / 96.29 vs 81.81 / 95.28 (Qwen); the triple editors score far lower (BLEU 26-62). Gains are largest on code (Llama-2 70.50 vs 50.78 BLEU) and math. They are not uniform across domains: fixed windows are higher on Llama-3.1 chemistry and poetry BERTScore (97.46 vs 97.16, 85.80 vs 84.78) and on Qwen biology and news BLEU.

Check that the gain holds on standard editing benchmarks. Setup: UnKE (unstructured knowledge as free-text question answering) and CounterFact (counterfactual factual updates) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, same baselines and metrics. Result: BLEU / BERTScore 81.57 / 96.03 vs 79.02 / 95.88 on UnKE and 90.69 / 98.29 vs 86.27 / 97.85 on CounterFact against fixed-window AnyEdit, with MEMIT and AlphaEdit at 21-32 BLEU.

Stress-test on longer, more tightly reasoned targets. Setup: build QwQ-Edit from 300 randomly chosen test items of a long chain-of-thought math dataset (GSM8K and MATH questions answered by QwQ-32B), most of them longer than the longest EditEverything sample and denser in reasoning words such as 'therefore' and 'since' (counted with a fixed word list); edit Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct with both segmentation schemes and bin results by answer length and by reasoning-word density. Result: surprisal boundaries score higher than fixed windows on both BLEU and BERTScore in every length bin and every density bin.

Check that the segmentation also helps a fine-tuning-based editor. Setup: replace the fixed-length chunks of the fine-tuning editor FT-UKE with surprisal boundaries on EditEverything, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Result: FT-UKE is already near ceiling (average BLEU 99.90 and 99.52) and surprisal segmentation nudges it to 99.95 and 99.57, with BERTScore unchanged or slightly higher; some domains go down (Qwen chemistry 99.78 to 99.05, poetry 100.00 to 98.60).

Test whether surprisal boundaries give more independent segments, which the least-squares update needs to avoid edits overwriting each other. Setup: on EditEverything, embed each segment with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and compute each sample's mean pairwise cosine between its segments; separately, extract the anchor keys at the editing layer of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for every segment and plot pairwise key similarity. Result: mean inter-segment similarity is 0.509 with surprisal boundaries against 0.594 with fixed windows, and key-similarity matrices are close to diagonal for surprisal boundaries while fixed windows show strong off-diagonal similarity between adjacent segments. Two worked examples show fixed windows splitting 'the product of | 2 and 3' and 'n = 34 / | 2', which surprisal boundaries keep intact.
